claims.text: Adding 1–3 atomic % boron or another metalloid to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
The microalloying addition will increase the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The proposed effect should occur at cooling rates typical of rapid solidification.
The proposed effect requires a microalloying concentration low enough to avoid secondary crystalline-phase formation.
Microalloying above a composition-dependent threshold may produce unwanted crystalline phases.
The microalloying element will increase local atomic-packing frustration.
The microalloying element will increase local chemical-bonding heterogeneity.
Increased packing frustration and bonding heterogeneity will disrupt long-range periodicity.
The added element will form energetically strong localized bonds, potentially with phosphorus and transition metals.
The microalloying addition will increase the alloy's overall atomic-size mismatch.
Strong localized bonding and increased atomic-size mismatch will raise the energetic barrier to crystalline nucleation during cooling.
The microalloying addition will retard atomic diffusion during subsequent thermal annealing.
Raising the crystalline-nucleation barrier will enhance glass-forming ability.
Retarding atomic diffusion during annealing will improve amorphous-state thermal stability.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate or a wider cooling-rate window for glass formation.
Relative to the unmodified alloy, the modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature.
The benefit may be negligible when other alloying elements dominate the bonding environment.
The benefit may be negligible when extremely rapid cooling already fully suppresses crystallization.
